name: find
summary: Search a directory tree for files by name, type, size, age or owner, and optionally act on them.

install.note: BusyBox find supports the common tests (-name, -type, -size, -mtime, -exec).

compat: Tests are evaluated left to right, and order matters. -print0, -delete and -iname are GNU/BusyBox extensions rather than strict POSIX.

examples.title: Find files by name pattern
examples.explain: Searches from the current directory (.) downward. Quote the pattern: unquoted, the shell would expand *.c in the current directory before find ever sees it.
options: Match the file name against a shell pattern (case-sensitive; -iname ignores case)

examples.title: Find files larger than 1 MiB
examples.explain: +1M means more than 1 MiB, -1M less than. Units: k (KiB), M (MiB), G (GiB). Note find rounds sizes up to whole units.
options: Regular files only (d = directories, l = symlinks)

examples.title: Large files on the whole root file system, hiding permission errors
examples.explain: -xdev stays on one file system (skips /proc, /sys and other mounts). -exec ls -lh {} + lists the matches with sizes. 2>/dev/null discards error messages such as 'Permission denied' for directories you cannot read; results you are allowed to see still print.
options: Do not descend into other mounted file systems
Run a command with the found paths as arguments
Send standard error (file descriptor 2) to the bit bucket

examples.title: Files modified in the last 24 hours
examples.explain: -mtime counts whole days: -1 means less than one day ago, +7 means more than seven days ago. Use -mmin -30 for the last 30 minutes.

examples.title: Search inside matching files
examples.explain: Runs grep -l on batches of .c files and prints the names of files containing main. {} is replaced by the file names; + passes many at once.
options: Run a command on the found files, batched

examples.title: Delete build objects after previewing them
examples.explain: Run the same command without -delete first and read the list. Only add -delete when the list is exactly what you want gone.
examples.warning: -delete removes files permanently and must be the LAST test. Placed before -name, it deletes everything find visits.

name: grep
summary: Search text for lines matching a pattern: in files, whole source trees, or command output.
compat: Exit status: 0 = a line matched, 1 = no match, 2 = error. That is why grep in a script or pipeline can 'fail' simply because nothing matched.

examples.title: Show matching lines with line numbers
examples.explain: Single quotes keep the shell from interpreting characters such as $ * [ in the pattern.
options: Prefix each match with its line number

examples.title: Search a source tree recursively
examples.explain: Searches every file below the current directory and prints file:line:text. Add -I to skip binary files.

examples.title: Only search C source and header files
examples.explain: --include limits the search to matching file names, which is much faster in a kernel or Yocto tree.
options: Only search files whose name matches the pattern (GNU)

examples.title: Case-insensitive search for several words
examples.explain: -E enables extended regular expressions, where | means OR. -i ignores upper/lower case.

examples.title: Hide comments and blank lines in a config file
examples.explain: -v inverts the match: print lines that do NOT match. The pattern matches lines that are empty or start with #.

examples.title: Search for a pattern that starts with a dash
examples.explain: Without --, grep would try to interpret -Wall as its own options. -- marks the end of options.

name: xargs
summary: Turn a list of names coming from a pipe into command-line arguments for another command.
compat: -0 and -I are supported by GNU and BusyBox. Without -0, names containing spaces or quotes are split incorrectly.

examples.title: Safely pass found files to another command
examples.explain: -print0 and -0 separate names with a NUL byte, so a file called 'file with spaces.txt' stays one argument.
options: find: end each name with NUL instead of newline

examples.title: Count lines in every C file
examples.explain: xargs runs wc -l with as many file names as fit on one command line and prints a total.

examples.title: Print each command before running it
examples.cmd: printf '%s\n' one two | xargs -t -I{} echo item {}
examples.explain: -I{} runs the command once per input line, replacing {}; -t prints each command to stderr first, which makes xargs behaviour visible.
options: Replace {} with each input line, one command per line
Print each command before executing it

name: which
summary: Show the full path of the program that runs when you type a command name.

install.note: Missing from some minimal images (e.g. Fedora containers). command -v is a builtin that always works.

compat: which only searches PATH; it does not know about aliases, functions or builtins. Use type -a to see everything.

examples.title: Find which gcc you are using
examples.explain: Prints a path such as /usr/bin/gcc. With several toolchains installed (host gcc vs a cross gcc from an SDK) this tells you which one PATH selects. Exit status is non-zero if nothing is found.

examples.title: List every match in PATH
examples.explain: Shows all copies in PATH order; the first one wins.
options: Print all matches, not just the first
